one_liner: General-purpose malloc(3) with per-thread arenas and decay-based purging; beats FreeBSD's phkmalloc under concurrency.
what_it_does: Drop-in replacement for the C allocator (malloc/calloc/realloc/free), built to avoid fragmentation and scale under concurrent allocation rather than optimize single-thread latency alone. On Linux/FreeBSD the public symbol prefix is empty by default, so it can replace libc's allocator directly (static/dynamic link or LD_PRELOAD); on macOS it overlays the malloc zone instead of replacing the symbols. It also exposes a non-standard extended API (mallocx/dallocx/sdallocx, mallctl) for arena control, heap profiling, and statistics that plain malloc doesn't offer.
how_it_is_fast: Splits the heap into multiple independent arenas (selected per-CPU or per-thread) so unrelated threads rarely contend on the same lock, backed by per-thread caches (tcache) that serve small size-class allocations without touching an arena at all. Size-class segregation limits fragmentation, and unused pages are reclaimed via time-based decay (dirty_decay_ms/muzzy_decay_ms) instead of immediate unmap, trading a little steady-state memory for fewer syscalls. The 5.4.0 release (Sep 2026) adds an HPA (huge-page-aware) extent allocator and demand-adaptive tcache refill/flush, replacing the older fixed-size tcache tuning knobs.
when_to_use: Multi-threaded servers/daemons with heavy concurrent alloc/dealloc (its own paper's use case: Redis-, MySQL-style workloads) where a single global heap lock serializes threads
Long-running processes where fragmentation avoidance over time matters more than the fastest possible single-thread malloc/free pair
You want built-in heap profiling/leak detection (--enable-prof, jeprof) instead of bolting on a separate tool
Target platform is Linux, FreeBSD, macOS, illumos, or Windows (all have dedicated CI workflows in the repo) and you're willing to link or LD_PRELOAD it
You're prepared to tune arena count / decay times / percpu_arena for your workload rather than accept the generic defaults
when_not_to_use: Single-threaded or low-concurrency programs, where multiple arenas can raise peak RSS without a throughput win (per the record's tradeoffs note)
Short-lived CLI tools where allocator warm-up and tuning overhead isn't worth it
You need documented, current jemalloc-vs-glibc numbers: README/TUNING.md carry no benchmarks, and the only numeric evidence in the repo's history is a 2006 phkmalloc/dlmalloc comparison
You want a simple mental model: open issues (#2688, #2751, #2808) show users struggling to reason about dirty/muzzy decay and HPA purging behavior in production

You're pinning a malloc_conf tuning string from before 5.4.0 — that release silently drops seven legacy tcache mallctls (lg_tcache_nslots_mul and friends), so an old config may stop tuning anything without an error

integration.form: source-drop, built via autoconf into a static or shared lib
integration.dependencies: none to build from a release tarball; autoconf is required only when building from a git/dev checkout (autogen.sh)
integration.min_toolchain: not documented — README/INSTALL.md give no minimum C standard or compiler version, only that autoconf is needed
integration.platforms: Linux, FreeBSD, macOS, illumos, Windows (per .github/workflows: linux-ci, freebsd-ci, illumos-ci, macos-ci, windows-ci); specific CPU architectures are not enumerated in the README
integration.thread_safety: not stated as a single explicit line, but the whole design (arenas, tcache, background threads) exists to serve concurrent multi-threaded allocation safely
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — explain: default symbol prefix is empty on Linux/FreeBSD (can replace malloc/free/calloc/realloc directly), but on macOS it overlays the malloc zone without replacing the symbols, and --with-jemalloc-prefix/--with-mangling exist specifically to avoid symbol collisions when it isn't used as a full drop-in

gotchas: Decay-based purging is a frequent confusion point: open issues report dirty_decay_ms 'not taking effect' (#2688) and ask for clearer docs on decay/purging (#2751), so memory isn't released back to the OS as immediately or predictably as a naive malloc
Retained/metadata memory can accumulate and has no obvious release path (#2675, 'How to release retained and metadata')
5.4.0 removed seven legacy tcache tuning mallctls (lg_tcache_nslots_mul, tcache_nslots_small_min/max, etc.); malloc_conf strings referencing them are now silently ignored rather than erroring
Under vm.overcommit_memory=2, vm.max_map_count can grow steadily from jemalloc's extent/arena mmap behavior (#1328), which matters for containers with strict map-count limits
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick jemalloc over mimalloc/snmalloc/TCMalloc when you need its mature jeprof heap-profiling and fine-grained arena/decay tuning knobs, or you're already on a codebase built around it (Redis, FreeBSD libc); the sibling entries' own numbers (mimalloc >2.5x faster than jemalloc on sh6bench, snmalloc ~4x glibc at 64 threads) suggest mimalloc or snmalloc are more likely to win a raw throughput shootout today.
verified_claims_summary: Evans' 2006 BSDCan paper (first-party, not peer-reviewed, no compiler/flags given, on a 4-CPU dual-dual AMD Opteron 275 / FreeBSD-CURRENT box) shows jemalloc beating FreeBSD's phkmalloc by roughly 1.1x-1.55x mean run time across five single-threaded programs (cca, gs, sh6bench, smlng, cfrac), and by roughly two orders of magnitude or more in throughput on a 20-thread malloc-test microbenchmark, where phkmalloc collapses below 1e5 allocs/sec by 10 threads while jemalloc plateaus near 3e7.
status_note: Actively maintained: 5.4.0 shipped Sep 17 2026 with 160+ commits and the dev branch was pushed the same day as this review; BSD-2-Clause licensed and small enough to vendor, but the repo itself carries no modern jemalloc-vs-glibc benchmark numbers.
